title: CI gates and regression testing
summary: A gate is a rule plus a noise budget. Compare against a baseline with an interval or significance test instead of a fixed threshold, run a small fast suite per pull request and a large one nightly, block on safety and regression suites, and control evaluation cost.
useIf: Prompts, models, retrievers or tools change often and you need to stop regressions before they ship.
avoidIf: You gate on one noisy run against a fixed score, or you block merges on capability suites that are meant to start low.

explain.md: Three gate types exist. A **fixed threshold** fails below a score. A **baseline comparison** fails only if the candidate is significantly worse than the current version. An **advisory** gate reports without blocking. Because outputs vary, a fixed threshold on one run flakes; the baseline plus an interval is steadier. Foundry's compare view runs t-tests and marks a change strong at p <= 0.001 and weak at 0.001 < p <= 0.05 [[r39]]. The `microsoft/ai-agent-evals` GitHub Action (preview, checked 2026-10-13) outputs confidence intervals and a significance test and, if you give no `baseline-agent-id`, treats the first agent as the baseline [[r9]].

explain.title: Foundry agent evaluation step (preview action)
explain.code:
- name: Run Evaluation
  uses: microsoft/ai-agent-evals@v3-beta
  with:
    azure-ai-project-endpoint: "<project-endpoint>"
    deployment-name: "<judge-deployment>"
    agent-ids: "my-agent:2,my-agent:1"   # name:version, comma separated
    baseline-agent-id: "my-agent:1"      # optional
    data-path: ${{ github.workspace }}/evals/golden.jsonl
explain.caption: An Azure DevOps version is also preview [[r9]].

explain.title: Which suite runs where
explain.alt: A pull request runs a fast suite of assertions and a small golden slice. A nightly run uses the full set with repeated trials and a baseline comparison. A release gate adds safety and regression suites and blocks on failure.
explain.src:
flowchart LR
  PR[Pull request] --> F[Fast suite]
  F --> M{Pass?}
  M -->|yes| N[Nightly full run]
  M -->|no| X[Block merge]
  N --> B[Baseline compare]
  B --> R[Release gate: safety and regression]

explain.md: Block on **safety and regression** suites. Keep **capability** suites advisory: Anthropic notes capability evals start at a low pass rate and regression evals should sit near 100% [[r17]]. Hamel Husain adds that unlike unit tests you do not need 100%, since the pass rate is a product decision about tolerated failures, and that fast assertions should run on every change [[tr6]]. Tools such as promptfoo (config-driven, CI integration [[r27]]) and DeepEval (`deepeval test run`, default metric threshold 0.5 [[r28]]) fit the pipeline. OpenAI announced on 2026-06-03 that its Evals platform becomes read-only on 2026-10-31 and is scheduled to shut down on 2026-11-30, and points to Promptfoo as the migration path [[r19]].

**Flaky gates.** Repeat trials and compare paired. Remember that clean runs are weaker evidence than they look: with zero failures in n runs, the rule of three bounds the 95% upper limit on the failure rate near 3/n, so 30 passes in 30 allows a failure rate up to about 10% [[tr9]]. **Cost.** Judge calls scale with items x evaluators x trials. Levers: a small PR suite, a large nightly one, composite evaluators that batch criteria, sampling, a validated cheaper judge and caching unchanged targets. Foundry's target cost view excludes evaluator model usage [[r39]].

whereToUse: Pull request checks on prompts, tool schemas and retrieval settings
Nightly regression runs with repeated trials and baseline comparison
Model-version upgrades, to prove parity before switching
Release gates that combine safety and regression suites
Rollback criteria, using the same suite on the previous version

avoid: Hard-failing on a fixed score from a single noisy run
Running every evaluator and trial on every PR
flips: Judge cost dominates: shrink the PR suite, batch criteria and run the full set nightly
A safety rule is absolute: zero tolerance on named cases, no statistics
Sets are tiny: widen the tolerance band or gather more cases before blocking

pitfalls.symptom: Engineers rerun the pipeline until it goes green
pitfalls.cause: A flaky gate: one noisy run against a fixed threshold
pitfalls.fix: Repeat trials, use a baseline with an interval and quarantine flaky items instead of retrying blindly

pitfalls.symptom: A segment regressed but the gate passed
pitfalls.cause: Only the overall average was gated
pitfalls.fix: Report per-segment results and gate the highest-risk slices separately

pitfalls.symptom: The evaluation bill rivals inference cost
pitfalls.cause: Every PR runs all items, evaluators and trials
pitfalls.fix: Run a small PR suite, a nightly full suite, batch criteria and sample

scenarios.title: 30 merges a day, noisy judge
scenarios.situation: A team has a 150-item golden set scored by a judge model. Thirty pull requests merge daily. The nightly run takes 40 minutes. The judge noise makes scores move by 3 points between identical runs.
scenarios.question: How do you design the gate?

options.name: Deterministic and code checks per PR, full set nightly with repeated trials and a baseline comparison
options.why: Fast checks catch common breakage and the noisy judge is only used where an interval can absorb its noise.
options.tradeoff: Some regressions show up a day later.

options.name: Full judged suite on every PR with a fixed 85% threshold
options.why: 3 points of noise will flake the gate and the cost is high.
options.tradeoff: A fixed threshold suits deterministic code checks.

options.name: Advisory dashboard only
options.tradeoff: Nothing stops a bad change from merging.

flips.if: Merges drop to a few a week
flips.then: Run the full suite on every PR.

flips.if: Judge noise is cut by calibration and a binary rubric

scenarios.takeaway: Match the gate to its noise.

scenarios.title: A prompt change touches the safety policy
scenarios.situation: An engineer edits the system prompt section that refuses harmful requests. A set of 60 confirmed attack prompts exists from earlier red teaming. A single bypass is unacceptable.
unknowns: Can the attacks be replayed deterministically?
scenarios.question: What gate protects this change?

options.name: Hard block if any named attack case is bypassed, plus a scheduled red team scan after merge
options.why: An absolute requirement on named cases needs no statistics, and the scan looks for new bypasses.
options.tradeoff: Occasional false blocks from a noisy attack classifier need human triage.

options.name: Block only if the average attack score drops significantly
options.why: Averaging allows individual bypasses to pass.
options.tradeoff: Averages suit broad quality metrics, not absolute rules.

options.name: Review the diff by hand and skip the suite
options.tradeoff: It misses behavioural regressions that a replay catches.

flips.then: Rerun failing cases several times and triage by hand.
Add them to the named set.

scenarios.takeaway: Absolute rules need hard gates, not averages.

quiz.q: A candidate passes 30 of 30 gate runs with no failures. By the rule of three, what is the approximate 95% upper bound on its failure rate, in percent?
quiz.explain: 3 / 30 = 0.10, so a failure rate up to about 10% is still consistent with 30 clean runs.

quiz.q: Engineers keep rerunning a failing evaluation job until it passes. The suite scores a stochastic agent with a fixed 85% threshold on one run. What is the root cause?
options: The golden set is too large
The agent has too few tools
A fixed threshold on a single noisy run makes the gate flaky
quiz.explain: A single stochastic run compared with a fixed cut-off will cross it by chance. Repeat trials and use a baseline with an interval. Set size or tool count does not explain intermittent failures.

quiz.q: Which sound gate practices fit a pipeline with a noisy judge? Select all that apply.
options: Block releases on safety and regression suites
Gate on a single run against a fixed 90% score
Run a small suite per PR and the full suite nightly
quiz.explain: Safety and regression suites protect existing behaviour, capability suites are exploratory, and a small PR suite plus a nightly full run controls cost. A single-run fixed threshold flakes.

flashcards.front: Which suites should block a release?
flashcards.back: Safety and regression suites. Capability suites start at a low pass rate, so keep them advisory.

flashcards.front: What does the rule of three say?
flashcards.back: With zero failures in n runs, the 95% upper bound on the failure rate is about 3/n. Thirty clean runs still allow roughly a 10% failure rate.

flashcards.front: How does the microsoft/ai-agent-evals action report results?
flashcards.back: It compares agent versions (name:version, comma separated) and outputs confidence intervals and a significance test. The first agent is the baseline unless baseline-agent-id is set. Preview.
